title: Hibernation: Not a Snooze
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant open with a request that listeners 'sandwich' their listening by also hearing the most recent episode, then discuss hibernation: how it differs from sleep, the physiological changes involved (heart rate, breathing, metabolism, hormones, set point, brown fat), and triggers such as temperature, food scarcity, photoperiod and circannual rhythm. They cover related states like estivation, brumation, and torpor, examples from bears, Arctic ground squirrels, lungfish, box turtles, chickadees, poor-wills and hummingbirds, and whether humans could hibernate, including NASA interest, hydrogen sulfide experiments on mice, the Russian lutka practice, and the yogi who reportedly lowered his heartbeat during an eight-day sealed stay. A listener mail segment about the wine industry's term 'wine growing' and a wine documentary closes the episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and listening 'sandwich' request
segments.summary: Hosts ask listeners who are catching up on old episodes to also listen to the most recent one, then chat about social media pages and cover bands.
topics: Stuff You Should Know social media

segments.title: Energy use, warm-bloodedness and what hibernation is
segments.summary: The hosts explain metabolic energy conversion and heat loss, the role of clothing in human spread, and define hibernation as a prolonged state of lowered body temperature and metabolism, noting bears are technically not true hibernators.

segments.title: Hibernation versus sleep and torpor
segments.summary: Hibernation is distinguished from sleep by drastic physiological change, a coma-like state, and sleep deprivation on waking. Torpor is discussed as both an umbrella term and a short daily state; estivation and brumation are introduced.

segments.title: Zoo animals and hibernation triggers
segments.summary: Zoo animals may be triggered to hibernate for a more natural cycle. Jurgen Aschoff's term Zeitgeber, meaning sleepy-time triggers, is introduced, with temperature as the main trigger.

segments.title: Google and Squarespace sponsor read
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Google and Squarespace offering a custom domain, business email and website for small businesses.

segments.title: Food supply, birds, photoperiod and circannual rhythm
segments.summary: Food scarcity and photoperiod (shortening days) act as triggers. Common poorwill is named as the only bird in true hibernation; other birds use daily torpor. Circannual rhythm is contrasted with circadian rhythm.

segments.title: Dens, food storage and fat-fueled hibernation
segments.summary: Animals prepare dens or shelters, sometimes partially exposed to weather. Some store food or fatten up heavily. Brown fat generates heat through non-shivering thermogenesis, and the set point regulates body temperature.

segments.title: Hormones and physiological changes
segments.summary: The endocrine system, including the pituitary, thyroid, insulin and melatonin, controls hibernation changes. Delta opioid (DADLE) is noted as inducing hibernation-like effects. Heart rate and breathing drop dramatically in chipmunks, bats, and box turtles.

segments.title: Waste, dehydration, estivation in lungfish and torpor in birds
segments.summary: Hibernating animals produce no feces and recycle urea, getting water from fat. Estivation is illustrated by lungfish encased in mucus cocoons. The chickadee's daily torpor and poor-will's seven-hour recovery are described, and hummingbirds are noted for high heart rates and daily torpor.

segments.title: Human hibernation, NASA and hydrogen sulfide research
segments.summary: Discussion of whether humans can hibernate, NASA interest in suspended animation for space travel, Lutka winter practice, Japanese man in the woods, the yogi study, and hydrogen sulfide experiments on mice by Mark Roth.

segments.title: Listener mail: wine growing
segments.summary: A listener writes about the term 'wine growing' and how wine grapes differ from table grapes, and the hosts discuss a wine documentary and a future wine episode.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: Hosts give social media handles, email address and website, and direct listeners to the howstuffworks site for more.
